list.listitem: Suspect intussusception in a child between the ages of 6 months and 2 years of age that presents with abdominal pain, irritability, vomiting and/or rectal bleeding/bloody stools. C

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion as presentation is variable; less than 50% of children have classic presentation of intermittent colicky abdominal pain, bloody (“currant jelly”) stools, and palpable “sausage” abdominal mass present. C
Ultrasound is the first-line diagnostic modality due to high diagnostic accuracy and lack of ionizing radiation. C
Recommended first-line treatment in a stable patient with no evidence of perforation/peritonitis is pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance. B
Surgical reduction is recommended if a patient is unstable, has evidence of perforation and/or peritonitis, or has unsuccessful attempted enema reduction. C

background.definition: Pediatric intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and young children (3 months to 6 years). It occurs when a portion of intestine (intussusceptum) telescopes into an adjacent portion (intussuscipiens), most commonly ileocolic. Usually it is idiopathic, but can occur at a pathologic lead point (an abnormal growth in the intestine). If untreated, it can lead to ischemia, which can result in bowel necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis. It is the second most common pediatric surgical emergency behind appendicitis.

list.listitem: Worldwide mean incidence of intussusception: 74 (range 9-328) per 100,000 children <1 year of age per year. Highest incidence is in Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, Israel, Vietnam, and South Korea.
In the best data available, incidence of pediatric intussusception in the US since 2000 is 35 per 100,000 children per year.
More than half of cases occur in children less than 12 months of age, with peak incidence at ages 5 to 9 months.
10-25% of cases occur in children greater than 2 years old.
Some studies report increased prevalence in spring and fall, while others found no seasonality.

Over 90% of cases are idiopathic with no clear causative lead point. It is postulated that temporary lymphatic engorgement or uncoordinated peristalsis from viral infection creates a physiologic lead point. A significant reduction in incidence during the COVID-19 pandemic supports this hypothesis. Adenovirus infection, particularly adenovirus C (often associated with respiratory symptoms), has consistently been shown to be associated with intussusception. HHV-6, enterovirus, COVID-19, and norovirus infection have also shown an association in some studies.
There is no statistically significant causative relationship of intussusception with wild-type rotavirus.
There is no statistically significant risk of intussusception following rotavirus vaccination (Rotarix, RotaTeq) based on two large randomized controlled trials.

Pathological lead point present in ~6%: more common in children <3 months or >5 years of age. Meckel diverticulum is the most common pathological lead point and others include IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), enteric duplication cyst, benign polyps, lymphoma, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, celiac disease, hemangiomas, vascular malformation, parasites, tumors, and inspissated stool in patients with cystic fibrosis.
There are some reports of iatrogenic cases of intussusception due to long enteral feeding tube, operative trauma, and post-operative.

A portion of intestine (intussusceptum) at a lead point telescopes into the adjacent portion (intussuscipiens) dragging mesentery into the intestinal lumen leading to venous and lymphatic congestion resulting in intestinal edema.

Most commonly occurs ileocolic (>80%) with the terminal ileum as intussusceptum telescoping into the ascending colon as the intussuscipiens. Hepatic flexure is the most common location. Small bowel intussusceptions are much less common and are often associated with pathological lead points.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: No clear seasonality in recent studies

list.listitem: Clinical diagnosis is challenging as presentation is variable and can mimic many other gastrointestinal disorders. C
The classic triad of abdominal pain, bloody stool, and palpable abdominal mass occurs infrequently at presentation. C
Ultrasound should be used as first-line diagnostic tool. C
Screening abdominal radiograph should not be performed. C
Presentation of pediatric intussusception is variable and has significant overlap with several other gastrointestinal disorders.
History and physical exam have low diagnostic accuracy with rate of misdiagnosis as high as 60%.
Classic presentation of intermittent colicky abdominal pain, bloody (“currant jelly”) stools, and palpable “sausage” abdominal mass occurs in only 4.3% to 40% of cases.
Up to 20% of patients present without abdominal pain.
Infants may present with irritability or crying and/or lethargy.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis detailed the diagnostic accuracy of history elements: abdominal pain (LR+ 1.14, LR- 0.65), vomiting (LR+ 1.49, LR- 0.44), rectal bleeding/bloody stools (LR+ 1.96, LR- 0.72).

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis detailed the diagnostic accuracy of PE findings: abdominal pain with palpation (LR+ 1.75, LR- 0.81), fecal blood/grossly positive stools (LR+ 3.36, LR- 0.48).

A 2025 prospective observational study identified 4 clinical variables (absence of fever, intermittent abdominal pain/irritability, absence of diarrhea, RUQ tenderness) that reliably predict the likelihood of intussusception and need for ultrasound evaluation.
Abdominal pain is the most common symptom in all ages and the strongest clinical predictors in infants <12 months are vomiting, irritability and blood in the stool.
Guaiac-positive/bloody stools were previously stated as highly predictive, but a recent study contradicts this; this is likely a late finding and therefore should not be used as a screening tool.
Ultrasound if first-line diagnostic modality due to its high diagnostic accuracy and lack of ionizing radiation.
A meta-analysis from 2023 found excellent diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound with LR+ 24.6 and LR- 0.05.
A 2026 systematic review and diagnostic meta-analysis showed excellent diagnosis accuracy of ultrasound with a pooled sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 96% (LR+ 24, LR- 0.04).
A second meta-analysis from 2022 also found excellent diagnostic accuracy for point-of-care ultrasound in the emergency department with LR+ 50 and LR- 0.05.

Typical ultrasound findings: peripheral hyperechoic ring with central echogenicity is called the target sign or donut sign (transverse view) and pseudokidney sign (longitudinal view); ileocolic seen in right abdomen with diameter of 2-4 cm; presence of mesenteric lymph nodes within lumen of intussuscipiens is highly specific.
Doppler showing absence of blood flow within intussusception correlates with bowel ischemia and necrosis at surgery and is predictive of unsuccessful enema reduction.
Abdominal radiography should not be used as the primary screening test for suspected intussusception, but could be used to assess for pneumoperitoneum prior to treatment.
Findings suspicious for intussusception: paucity of gas in right lower quadrant, intracolonic soft tissue mass, absence of cecal gas.
Low diagnostic accuracy with LR+ 2.5 and LR- 0.20.

In limited resource areas where ultrasound is not available, a pediatric intussusception score (PIS) in combination with abdominal radiography data and common manifestations improves diagnostic sensitivity.
Laboratory
Ischemia-modified albumin may be a marker useful to screen for bowel obstruction, but requires prospective validation before being adopted.
The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio may be a useful predictor of need for surgical treatment, but requires prospective validation before being adopted.

A 2026 systematic review suggests several biomarkers (WBC, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, CRP, cytokines, serum lactate, D-dimer, electrolytes) are useful to assess severity. Some novel molecular markers (I-FABP, MCP-1 amd transfer RNA fragments) may enhance early diagnosis and outcome prediction, but this requires prospective validation before being adopted.
Suspect in child <2 years of age presenting with abdominal pain, irritability, vomiting and/or rectal bleeding/bloody stools.
Perform abdominal ultrasound and proceed to management as below if evidence of intussusception and/or no other pathology to explain symptoms identified.
See for a suggested management algorithm.
Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance is the gold standard non-surgical treatment.B
Pneumatic enema reduction may be more successful than hydrostatic enema reduction, but is more expensive and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.B
If the patient is unstable or there is evidence of peritonitis, proceed directly to surgical reduction. C
If the patient is stable, consider delayed repeated enema reduction. If unsuccessful, surgical reduction is necessary. B
Consider outpatient management (discharge from ED) after enema reduction if the patient meets certain criteria. C
Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to reduction is not recommended.B.
APSA 2020 guidelines concluded that prophylactic antibiotic administration prior to enema reduction is not recommended as it does not appear to reduce post-reduction complications.

Dexamethasone plus enema reduction was not significantly more effective than enema reduction alone in reducing recurrence in a Cochrane Review of two trials with 218 participants (RR 1.09, 95% CI: 0.94 to 1.26).

A 2025 single-center prospective randomized control trial showed that a single IV dose of methylprednisolone successfully treated children ages 0- to 4 ears with symptoms <for less than24 hours compared to observation alone (812 vs 56.), NNT = 4, particularly for ileocolic intussusception (77. vs 22.), NNT = 2, but this requires more prospective validation before being adopted.
A 2024 meta-analysis showed that sedation can increase the success rate of radiologic enema reduction in children with ileocolic intussusception without increased risk of perforation.

A 2023 cross-sectional study of 3203 patients showed opioid analgesia and sedation are not commonly used in children undergoing ileocolic intussusception reduction, but neither was associated with intestinal perforation or failed reduction. A secondary analysis of this study showed specifically that fentanyl administration prior to reduction attempt was not associated with failed reduction.

There is no current evidence to support preference of surgical method (laparoscopic versus open reduction), but laparoscopic should be considered as the initial approach given the shorter lengths of hospitalization and equivalent complication rates.
If the patient is unstable or there is evidence of peritonitis, it is recommended to go directly to surgical management, either laparoscopic or open reduction.
If the patient is stable with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis, but non-surgical reduction is unsuccessful, it is recommended to perform surgical management.

A duration of abdominal pain greater than 48 hours, the presence of abdominal distension, presence of abdominal lump, and presence of red currant jelly stools are strong predictors of need for surgical management.

A 2026 single-center retrospective observational study showed that failure of ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema reduction is the strongest predictor of a pathological lead point and need for surgical evaluation.
Surgical resection is needed in 3-8% of cases.

A 2024 retrospective study identified several risk factors that predict the need for bowel resection. They include extended duration of symptoms (OR 2.1), presence of gross bloody stool (OR 8.9), elevated C-reactive protein levels (OR 4.8), lactate clearance rate (OR 17), and intussusception location (OR 13). These factors were combined into a comprehensive scoring system that can be used to predict the need for bowel resection.

Pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic (water-soluble contrast/saline) enema reduction is the recommended first-line therapy for patients who are stable. Air or liquid is introduced into the bowel via the rectum and pressure reduces the “telescoped” bowel to its normal position with real-time observation with fluoroscopy or ultrasound.

Pneumatic air enema reduction is commonly performed under fluoroscopic-guidance leading to exposure to ionizing radiation and is more expensive, but is cleaner, with lower risk of peritoneal contamination in the event of perforation.

Hydrostatic enema reduction is commonly performed under ultrasound guidance (no ionizing radiation), but requires a radiologist experienced in ultrasound. It is cheaper, messier, with similarly low perforation rates, but there is a higher risk of peritoneal contamination in the event of perforation

A 2015 meta-analysis of observational studies with over 32,000 children found a higher success rate with pneumatic enema compared with hydrostatic reduction (82.7% vs 69.6%), with no difference in the perforation rate.

A 2024 meta-analysis of retrospective studies with over 9,300 children found significantly shorter time to reduction, higher rate of successful reduction, and reduced length of hospital stay, lower overall complication rate, and lower incidence of perforation with ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema reduction.
A 2025 systematic review suggests no significant difference in reduction techniques in terms of success rate and complications, with possible advantage of pneumatic over hydrostatic reduction.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis showed no significant difference between pneumatic and hydrostatic reduction in perforation rate, recurrence rate, length of hospital stay, reduction pressure, and fluoroscopy time, but found pneumatic to be more successful and quicker.

A 2023 single-center prospective study over 15 years showed ultrasound-guided pneumatic reduction is well-tolerated, simple, safe, and effective with a high success rate, no complications, and no ionizing radiation.
A 2023 randomized-control trial showed that ultrasound-guided pneumatic reduction was comparable with saline hydrostatic reduction in effectiveness and safety, but pneumatic may be faster.

A 2020 meta-analysis and 2024 randomized-control trial showed that fluoroscopy-guided pneumatic enema and ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema were equally successful and safe for reduction of intussusception.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis suggests several factors that predict decreased probability of successful enema reduction, including longer duration of symptoms, absence of abdominal pain, age younger than 1 year, presence of fever, rectal bleeding, and vomiting and ultrasound findings of ascites, left-sided intussusception, and trapped fluid.

A 2026 retrospective cohort study identified 7 independent predictors of failure of hydrostatic enema reduction: age < 1 year, vomiting, prolonged symptom duration, large target mass, transverse colon location, compromised mural perfusion, and marked bowel-wall edema.
A 2023 retrospective cohort study showed ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema reduction is safe and effective in idiopathic intussusception with history of symptoms ≥ 48 hours.

A 2020 guideline and systematic review from the American Pediatric Surgical Association (APSA) concluded that at the time of enema reduction, a physician capable of abdominal decompression of pneumoperitoneum and CPR should be present. The guideline recommends waiting between 30 minutes to 4 hours prior to repeated attempts at delayed enema reduction. It also recommends observation for recurrence for 4 hours after reduction of ileocolic intussusception.
Delayed repeated attempts can be considered in a stable patient when partial reduction is achieved on initial attempt, and are successful in up to 50% of cases.

A 2025 multicenter retrospective cohort study showed a repeat reduction attempt is recommended in hemodynamically stable children who fail initial ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction, ideally within 60 minutes, with no more than 3 total attempts. Sonographic monitoring of bowel wall edema and perfusion should be used to guide decisions about repeated attempts.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of children who had successful enema reduction showed outpatient management (discharge from ED) may be safe and is recommended post-reduction if the patient meets the following criteria: normal hemodynamics, asymptomatic, tolerance of enteral intake, absence of comorbidities necessitating hospitalization, and reliable caretakers with means to return to the ED.
If the patient does not meet the above criteria or requires surgical reduction, hospitalization is recommended.
Complications include recurrence and intestinal perforation leading to peritonitis and possible sepsis.

Risk of recurrence within 48 hours is low. In a 2014 meta-analysis, the overall recurrence rate after fluoroscopic-guided pneumatic enema was 8.5% (95% CI: 6.9-10.4%) and after ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema reduction was 7.5% (95% CI: 5.7-9.8%).
A 2025 single-center retrospective analysis of 215 cases found that ultrasound-guided hydrostatic enema reduction for recurrent intussusception is safe and effective.

A 2025 scoping systematic review found that recurrent intussusception does not seem to be associated with a pathological lead point, and should be managed similarly to a primary occurrence with non-operative management.
The mean perforation rate for intussusception reduction is 0.8%.
Mortality in the US is low due to safe and effective treatments and is 2.1 per 1 million live births. B

In low- and middle-income countries, surgery is the mainstay of treatment and there is a high rate of bowel resection with resulting high morbidity and mortality due in part to delayed presentations and late referral. B
In a 2023 review, risk of recurrence was higher in adenovirus-related intussusception (48.1%) compared to without adenovirus (13.8%) (OR 5.8, 95% CI 1.6-21.2%).

In a 2023 retrospective review of 624 children, age greater than 1 year-old, secondary intussusception, and mesenteric lympadenopathy were identified as independent risk factors for in-hospital recurrence after successful reduction with air enema.

cell.label: Operative management. If patient is hemodynamically stable, start with laparoscopic reduction. Consider intraoperative use of air or saline enema to facilitate reduction. Consider removing the appendix in setting of inflammation or ischemia.
4 hours observation to ensure symptoms resolved and tolerating oral regimen
Repeat enema if patient is stable, without peritonitis; repeat up to 4 attempts.
Hospital admission (poor oral intake, vomiting, lethargy, fever, tachycardia, and/or pain; difficulty returning to ED after discharge).
